handback.t:
READ-ONLY RESEARCH: detention and accessorial money (as of 2026-10-10). Standard depth, about 9 searches, no page fetches.

Process caveats:
- I wrote no marker file and stored nothing, per your read-only rule. The ADR-438 marker, AIDefence scan and acceptance steps were skipped, so `screened=false`. Spend is unmeasured.
- Everything below comes from search-result summaries, not primary documents. Grades are capped accordingly.
- I did NOT research these sub-questions: state detention laws, the Norwegian vegfraktloven text, and CMR waiting-time rules (only a thin Norway/e-CMR hit). I also did not research the small-carrier share or the 2h/cap/notice norms beyond the sources below.

**Premise correction:** I found no "OIG 2024 detention report". The DOT OIG report is from 2018 (see the OIG/J.J. Keller item below). The ATRI study is 2024 and covers 2023 data.

**Key facts**
- ATRI 2024 (2023 data): detention hit about 39.3% of stops (reefer about 56%), and 4.9% of stops ran over 4 hours. Carriers invoiced only about 75% of the time, and about 55% of those invoices were paid. That means roughly 41% of detention events yield payment. Cost was $11.5B lost productivity plus $3.6B direct unreimbursed, about $15.1B in total. Sources: https://www.ttnews.com/articles/atri-driver-detention-2023, https://www.trucknews.com/transportation/truck-driver-detention-costs-industry-15-billion-in-2023-atri, https://www.freightwaves.com/news/new-study-shows-detention-improving-slightly-but-still-pervasive. Grade: High on the numbers. Medium on interpretation, because the $15.1B is mostly lost productivity, not claimable cash. Only the roughly $3.6B direct cost is recoverable in principle.
- OIG 2018: no reliable industry-wide detention data exists. A 15-minute increase in facility time raises crash rate 6.2%. Source: https://www.jjkeller.[REDACTED:high_entropy]. Grade: High. The OIG also later said FMCSA's study plan may not be representative: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/fmcsa-details-new-truck-driver-detention-time-survey.
- FMCSA's detention study (about 80 carriers, 2,500 drivers, 12 months, ELD/TMS data) is a data-collection effort only. The study is not a rule. I found nothing on a 2025-26 federal detention rule. Grade: Medium, absence of evidence.
- The INVEST Act proposal included a rulemaking on limits on uncompensated detention and a public data site. As far as I found, it never became law. Source: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/lawmakers-prod-fmcsa-to-move-on-driver-detention. Grade: Medium.
- Industry comment suggested 2 free hours, then $100/hr. This is a norm and a proposal, not law. Source: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/truckers-push-fmcsa-to-make-brokers-pay-for-detention-time. Grade: Medium.
- Broker transparency: the 2024 NPRM drew about 7,000 comments, with no final rule. A second NPRM was planned. It would give carriers 48-hour access to transaction records and void waiver clauses. Sources: https://www.logisticsmgmt.com/article/fmcsa_reopens_comment_period_for_broker_transparency_focused_nprm/Brokers, https://www.bobtail.com/blog/broker-transparency-2025-what-new-fmcsa-rules-mean-for-carriers-and-owner-operators/. Grade: Medium. Check the current status before building on it.
- Norway ratified the e-CMR protocol, and e-CMR is used on Norwegian transport orders. The Mobility Package is being implemented step by step. Source: https://trans.info/en/norway-ratifies-the-e-cmr-protocol-this-is-the-26th-country-to-rely-on-electronic-transport-documents-189755. CMR has no waiting-time sanction. Delay claims need proven damage and are capped at 1x the freight charge. Source: https://trans.info/en/limit-of-liability-of-the-carrier-for-the-delay-167984. Grade: Medium.
- Shipper side: invoice error rates are cited at 5-15% (vendor blogs, so Low-Medium). Accessorials are the main error category. Examples are detention billed inside free time, wrong rate or hours, duplicate bills from both carrier and broker, and liftgate fees where the dock has forklifts. Sources: https://www.kognitos.com/blog/freight-audit/, https://www.lojistic.com/blog/freight-invoice-auditing-common-errors-that-inflate-shipping-costs.
- Denial reasons and winning evidence: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/understanding-detention-pay-clauses, https://www.thetruckersreport.com/truckingindustryforum/threads/whats-the-1-reason-your-detention-claims-get-denied-poll.2529156/page-3, https://otrucking.com/resources/guides/detention-time-and-pay/. Several are vendor or forum sources. Grade: Medium-Low.

**Top 8 pains, ranked by money x frequency (my ranking is judgment)**
1. Detention never invoiced, or invoiced late. About 25% of events are never billed (ATRI). Frequency is highest and it is the cheapest to fix. High.
2. Invoiced but unpaid. About 45% of invoices go unpaid (ATRI). High.
3. No detention clause in the rate confirmation, or terms that differ from the contract. Brokers deny on this basis. Medium.
4. Missed notice or documentation windows, often 24-72h. Medium.
5. Weak or single-source timestamps (driver-only claims). Medium.
6. The broker does not pass detention through when the shipper pays it, and transparency rules are not final. Medium-Low. Evidence is mostly advocacy and anecdote.
7. Reefer and specialized freight has the highest incidence (reefer about 56% of stops) but is paid less often. High on incidence.
8. Lumpers and other accessorials with receipt and authorization disputes. Low. I found no quantified source.

**Winning-evidence checklist**
- The rate confirmation or contract showing free time, hourly rate and when the clock starts (gate arrival or dock check-in).
- ELD/GPS geofence arrival and departure events.
- A second independent timestamp, such as a gate log, facility check-in or photo. Two independent sources beat one authoritative one.
- A signed BOL/POD with in and out times.
- Contemporaneous notice to the broker or shipper at the time of delay, not at invoicing.
- An invoice sent inside the stated deadline, with the supporting documents attached.
- For lumpers, the receipt and the shipper or consignee authorization (inferred, not sourced).

**5 product implications possibly missed**
1. Pre-emptive, real-time notification. Send a timed notice the minute free time expires, since the notice clause is the commonest procedural kill.
2. Rate-con and contract clause extraction, with a go/no-go score for each load before any claim work. Contingency economics depend on terms existing.
3. Broker and shipper payment scoring. Learn which payers actually pay, and price contingency to match.
4. A shipper-side "defense" product. Audit carrier accessorials for detention billed inside free time, duplicates, and invoices where the broker and carrier both bill. This reuses the same evidence engine. Error-rate figures are vendor claims, so validate them.
5. Capture of the roughly 25% never billed. Automatically generate the invoice from ELD data, which is a stronger wedge than dispute work.

**Confidence overall:** High on the ATRI numbers. Medium on mechanics and evidence. Low on state laws, EU/Norway detail, small-carrier share, and shipper-defense market size. Next steps: fetch the ATRI PDF for the small-carrier split, check state laws, read the vegfraktloven and CMR text, and confirm the broker rule status.

Approval needed: nothing was stored. Tell me if you want this persisted to the `research` namespace.
